transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Weeks before the midterm elections take place
when voters will determine control of Congress,
the Labor Department says the economy added fewer jobs
than expected last month as the unemployment rate ticked
up to 4.2 percent.
Betsy Stevenson is a professor of economics and public policy
at the University of Michigan and was a member
of President Obama's Council of Economic Advisors.
>> People who are doing well are still doing well.
And any kind of worker who's struggling to get their foot
in the door, keep their foot in the door,
get a promotion to the next thing,
those are the people who are really struggling right now.
And I think that's why we're seeing this real increasing
anger over the labor market because there's no openings
and breaks for people to get.
>> Speaking there on NPR's weekend edition,
the Trump administration is mailing out $500 checks
to almost a million Americans who are enrolled
in certain private health insurance plans.
As NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports, the money comes
from fees collected from health insurance companies.
>> The group of people receiving the checks live in one
of the 30 states that use healthcare.gov
as their Obamacare website and make too much money
to receive premium subsidies.
>> Cynthia Cox directs the program on the Affordable Care
Act at the health research organization KFF.
>> Essentially what the Trump administration is doing is
taking some user fee dollars that insurance companies have paid
to the federal government to operate healthcare.gov.
>> Usually that money is used for community groups
who help people understand their options and enroll.
But the Trump administration has slashed funding
for those groups and is now sending out checks instead.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
>> A federal judge has ordered an immediate halt
to all border-related construction
in the Big Bend region of Texas,
and that includes Big Bend National Park.
Mary Cantrell from Marfa Public Radio reports the emergency
injunction will remain in effect while a lawsuit moves forward.
>> The Center for Biological Diversity,
a church restoration group, and a river guide are suing the
federal government over its border wall plans.
The judge's order says the Big Bend region is not necessarily
an area of high legal entry,
as federal waivers fast-tracking the project have claimed.
Anti-wall advocates, including Susan Hayes,
celebrated outside of a federal courthouse in El Paso.
>> The government had no justification legally
to issue the waivers in the first place.
It's what we all knew, to say that there is an emergency
with immigration or border security
and the greater Big Bend is complete and utter BS.
>> If the Trump administration appeals,
the case will go to the U.S. Supreme Court.
For NPR News, I'm Mary Cantrell in El Paso.
>> You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Tennessee's state prison chief Frank Strada has resigned
that over overseeing the failed execution
of Krista Pike this week.
Governor Bill Lee says Strada will leave this month
and independent review is scheduled to try to determine
what went wrong in the administration of two doses
to Pike, one of the drugs that Tennessee uses
to execute prisoners.
Her attorney says she's hospitalized in a coma
and on a ventilator and that hospital staff is working
to save her life.
Under Strada, the prison system also failed
to execute another convicted murderer, Tony Carruthers.
He came to Tennessee from Arizona,
where he oversaw three botched executions similar to Pike's.
>> A new study shows that eating
with another person just might help you manage
your blood sugar.
Researchers gave two groups of participants the same amount
of bread to eat and then measured how their blood sugar rose
and recovered, and Piers, barely McCoy, reports.
>> In one group, the participants ate their bread alone.
In the other, someone else was in the room,
and they found the social eaters recovered quicker.
That is, their blood sugar didn't spike as high
or came back down quicker, or both.
Lead author and behavioral neuroscientist,
Sheer Adzeel, says this might be
because humans are social animals.
>> If my brain develops in a social context, my brain learns
to regulate my glucose levels in social proximity.
>> She says other people may be a social cue the brain uses
to start processing sugar earlier, for example,
by releasing insulin, which helps regulate blood sugar.
The results appear in the journal Science Advances,
Burley McCoy, NPR News.
>> This is NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: Labor Department reports economy added fewer jobs than expected, unemployment rises to 4.2 percent
Trump administration mails $500 checks to nearly one million Americans in private health insurance plans
Federal judge halts all border wall construction in Big Bend region of Texas immediately
Tennessee prison chief Frank Strada resigns after failed execution of inmate Krista Pike
Study shows eating with another person helps regulate blood sugar levels better
